# Two Different Sources of Ambiguity

A model is identifiable when distinct parameter values imply distinct
distributions for the observable data. Formally, for a parameter $\theta$ and
observed-data law $P_\theta$,

$$
P_\theta=P_{\theta'}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\theta=\theta'.
$$

For a finite mixture,

$$
p(y\mid\Theta)=\sum_{k=1}^K\pi_k f(y\mid\theta_k),
$$

permuting component indices leaves the density unchanged. For every permutation
$\sigma$ of $1,\ldots,K$,

$$
\sum_{k=1}^K\pi_k f(y\mid\theta_k)
=
\sum_{k=1}^K\pi_{\sigma(k)}f(y\mid\theta_{\sigma(k)}).
$$

This **label nonidentifiability** is unavoidable: “component 1” is only a name.
It should be distinguished from deeper nonidentifiability, in which genuinely
different unordered mixtures produce the same observed distribution. Many
classical finite mixtures, including finite normal mixtures under appropriate
minimal representations, are identifiable *up to permutation*. That is enough
to identify the mixing distribution, but not the arbitrary numbering of its
atoms.

# Structural, Practical, and Label Identifiability

Three issues are often conflated:

| Issue | Meaning | More data under the same design? |
|---|---|---|
| Structural nonidentifiability | different scientifically distinct parameter values imply exactly the same observed law | no |
| Weak or practical identification | distributions differ, but only slightly over the observed range | sometimes |
| Label nonidentifiability | a permutation changes names but not the unordered mixture | no, because names are arbitrary |

Weak identification can occur when component means are close, a mixing weight is
near zero, or covariates provide little overlap. The likelihood then has broad
ridges or nearly equivalent modes. This is not repaired by relabeling; the data
contain little information about the separation itself.

When two components coincide, a nominal $K$-component model has a nonminimal
representation. For example,

$$
\pi f(y\mid\theta)+(1-\pi)f(y\mid\theta)=f(y\mid\theta),
$$

so $\pi$ is not identified. Likewise, a zero-weight component has parameters
that do not affect the observed distribution. These singular points are why
ordinary information-matrix and chi-squared approximations can fail in mixtures.

# Label Switching in Bayesian Computation

Suppose component priors are exchangeable. The prior and likelihood are then
invariant to every label permutation, so the posterior has $K!$ symmetric modes:

$$
p(\Theta\mid y)=p(\sigma\Theta\mid y).
$$

An MCMC chain may remain in one labeling or move among several. If it explores
the symmetric posterior correctly, the marginal posterior distribution of
$\mu_1$ is the same as that of $\mu_2$ in a two-component mixture. The raw
posterior mean

$$
E(\mu_1\mid y)=E(\mu_2\mid y)
$$

can lie between the two fitted component locations and describe neither
component. This is the **label-switching problem**: component-specific summaries
are meaningless until the target and labeling convention are defined.

A chain that never switches is not necessarily correct or incorrect. It may be
trapped in one symmetric mode, or it may deliberately use an asymmetric
parameterization. Standard trace plots and $\widehat R$ can therefore mislead:
chains in different permutations can look inconsistent even when their implied
mixture densities agree, while chains trapped in the same mode can hide other
non-permutation modes.

# Decide Which Quantities Need Labels

Many useful targets are invariant to permutation and require no relabeling:

- the mixture density and predictive distribution;
- the unordered set of component parameters and weights;
- the number of occupied components, when that target is well defined;
- co-clustering probabilities
  $P(Z_i=Z_j\mid y)$;
- posterior similarity matrices; and
- losses minimized over all permutations.

For clustering, the posterior similarity matrix

$$
S_{ij}=P(Z_i=Z_j\mid y)
$$

is label invariant because whether two observations share a component does not
depend on the component's name. A partition can be selected to approximate
$S$, while uncertainty remains visible in its off-diagonal probabilities.

Component-specific claims do require an explicit definition. “The component
with the lower mean” is a mathematical convention. “The activated T-cell state”
is a scientific definition that should use prespecified markers or external
information and be checked across samples.

# Ordering Constraints: Useful but Not Neutral

A common device imposes

$$
\mu_1<\mu_2<\cdots<\mu_K.
$$

For a univariate mixture with well-separated locations, this selects one of the
$K!$ equivalent labelings and can make summaries convenient. It does not create
information, resolve overlapping components, or prove that the ordered groups
have scientific meaning.

Ordering can be fragile when:

- components differ mainly in variance, shape, or a multivariate direction;
- component locations cross as a covariate changes;
- posterior mass includes nearly tied means;
- the chosen ordering variable is scientifically arbitrary; or
- different samples require incompatible orders.

An asymmetric prior or anchor observations can also assign labels, but then the
asymmetry is substantive model information. Sensitivity to the anchor or prior
must be reported rather than described as identification supplied by the data.

# Relabeling Posterior Draws

When component-specific summaries are genuinely needed, post-processing can
choose a permutation $\sigma_s$ for each posterior draw $s$. A generic rule
solves

$$
\sigma_s
=\arg\min_{\sigma\in\mathcal S_K}
L(\sigma\Theta^{(s)},\Theta^*),
$$

where $L$ is a declared loss and $\Theta^*$ is a reference or iteratively updated
template. Alternatives align allocation probabilities, minimize posterior
expected loss, or match components to scientifically anchored profiles.

Relabeling changes summaries, not the likelihood or information in the data. A
good procedure should:

1. state the target and loss;
2. give the same invariant predictions before and after relabeling;
3. remain stable across reasonable references and initializations;
4. expose rather than conceal overlapping or split components; and
5. propagate assignment uncertainty into downstream analyses.

Sorting every draw is one relabeling method, but it is appropriate only when the
sort variable defines the intended target throughout the posterior.

# Frequentist Fitting Has the Same Symmetry

Label switching is not uniquely Bayesian. A likelihood optimizer can return any
permutation of the same solution, and separate starts may number components
differently. Before comparing fits, align components or compare label-invariant
quantities such as log-likelihood, fitted density, and optimal matched parameter
sets.

Uncertainty is nonregular near coincident components or zero weights. The
observed information may be nearly singular, Wald intervals may be misleading,
and a usual parametric bootstrap may return permuted or split solutions. Bootstrap
replicates should be matched under a prespecified loss, and failure to obtain a
stable match is itself evidence of weak component-specific identification.

# Worked Example

Consider a two-component normal mixture with exchangeable priors:

$$
Y_i\sim
0.4\,\operatorname{Normal}(-2,1)
+0.6\,\operatorname{Normal}(2,1).
$$

One posterior mode places $(\mu_1,\mu_2)$ near $(-2,2)$; the symmetric mode
places it near $(2,-2)$. Averaging raw labeled draws can give both posterior means
near zero. Yet every draw may imply nearly the same bimodal predictive density.

If the scientific target is the lower-expression state, define

$$
\mu_{\mathrm{low}}=\min(\mu_1,\mu_2),
\qquad
\mu_{\mathrm{high}}=\max(\mu_1,\mu_2).
$$

These derived quantities are label invariant. If instead activation is defined
by several markers, ordering one marker is insufficient: components should be
matched to an externally defined marker profile, and ambiguous matches should
remain uncertain.

# Bioinformatics Design and Interpretation

Suppose a mixture is used to identify cell states across control and treated
specimens. Fitting each specimen separately can make numerical labels change
across specimens. A component called “2” in one donor has no inherent relation
to component “2” in another. Joint modeling, shared marker definitions, or
post-hoc matching may align states, but each imposes assumptions about which
features are conserved.

The treatment estimand might be a donor-level change in the proportion of an
anchored state. Donors are the experimental units; cell assignments are latent
measurements nested within donors. A downstream test that treats assigned cells
as error-free independent replicates ignores both assignment uncertainty and
within-donor dependence.

Statistically, identification means that the observed-data distribution can
distinguish the target under the model. Biologically, a reproducible component
still requires a defensible phenotype, design-aware replication, and external
validation. Neither a tight posterior conditional on an identifying constraint
nor a stable optimizer supplies biological identity by itself.

# Diagnostic and Sensitivity Workflow

| Question | Evidence | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Is the fitted density stable? | predictive distributions across chains, starts, and permutations | compare invariant quantities first |
| Are components separated? | responsibility entropy, parameter contrasts, likelihood profiles | report overlap; simplify or redesign if weak |
| Is uncertainty only a permutation? | match modes and compare after optimal permutation | retain all substantively different modes |
| Does the labeling convention matter? | ordered, anchored, and loss-based summaries | report sensitivity and define labels explicitly |
| Are tiny or duplicate components present? | near-zero weights, coincident parameters, singular curvature | reconsider $K$; regularize; avoid Wald inference |
| Are states reproducible across units? | donor- and batch-stratified fits; external markers | use hierarchical alignment and independent validation |
| Is downstream inference design-aware? | experimental-unit map and uncertainty propagation | aggregate or model at the independent-unit level |

Also inspect whether posterior computation moves among substantively distinct
solutions, not merely permutations. Relabeling all modes into one template can
incorrectly merge different explanations of the data.

# Common Misinterpretations

- **“An ordering constraint solves identifiability.”** It chooses names; it does
  not separate overlapping components or validate their interpretation.
- **“Label switching means MCMC failed.”** Switching can be correct exploration
  of a symmetric posterior. Failure is diagnosed on the target distribution,
  not raw component names alone.
- **“No switching means identification.”** A chain may simply be trapped in one
  of several modes.
- **“A component is a discovered class.”** Components may be devices for density
  approximation and can change with $K$ or the component family.
- **“Hard labels remove uncertainty.”** They hide it. Membership probabilities
  and donor-level replication remain relevant downstream.

- Hidden Markov models, developed later in this level, carry related state-label
  issues into dependent latent sequences.

Mixture parameters should be interpreted as an unordered collection unless a
scientific or mathematical convention defines their labels. Label switching is
permutation symmetry, not automatically computational failure. Work with
invariant targets whenever possible; when labels matter, declare and test the
relabeling rule. No labeling method repairs weak separation, singular components,
incorrect experimental units, or an unsupported biological interpretation.
